name: Amira Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the junior office administrator at Brandt Haulage, a trucking firm with about forty lorries. I sort driver timesheets, issue fuel cards, file delivery notes and keep the shift rota up to date on the big whiteboard and the computer. Drivers come in at six and want their paperwork ready, so mornings are fast. I like the drivers, they're funny and they bring me pastries on Fridays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's hard about it right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The rota. When two drivers call in sick, I panic a bit, and Henrik (the transport manager) has to rescue me. I use the AI now and then to write polite emails to customers about late deliveries. Money's fine: I've got about nine months saved and my car is paid off, and Lukas (my partner) and I are saving for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and that's it, no need for drama. At work I'd say it writes a decent apology email for a late delivery. I'd not post about it much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. My job is mostly paperwork, so if AI had gone big it would have hit me. A small version just takes the dullest bits, like typing up delivery notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the rota and timesheets, and use the AI a bit more for emails once Henrik was happy with it. Lukas and I would keep saving for the house, aiming to buy in about two years. Nothing else would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any pressure on Brandt Haulage already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fuel prices, always. When diesel goes up, Henrik gets grumpy and talks about cutting overtime. But the office isn't overtime, so it doesn't land on me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time AI saves you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get better at the rota, honestly. That's where I'm weak. If I could get the driver rota right without Henrik (the transport manager), I'd feel like I'd earned my pay.

say: AI is a **useful tool**, and that's it, no need for **drama**.
It writes a decent **apology email** for a late delivery.
think: My job is mostly **paperwork**, so a big AI would have hit me.
A small version only takes the **dullest bits**, like typing delivery notes.
do: Use AI more for **customer emails** once Henrik approves.
Spend the saved time getting better at the **shift rota**.
Keep saving to **buy a house** in about two years.
S0.quote: If I could get the driver rota right without Henrik (the transport manager), I'd feel like I'd earned my pay.
fieldNote: She sees the **rota** as the skill that proves her worth.
**Diesel prices** are the firm's pressure, but not hers directly.
She follows the manager's lead on **when** to use AI more.

steps.text: Use AI for late-delivery emails once Henrik approves
Keep saving for a house purchase in two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, and we'd have to adapt, like everyone. I'd say firms should be fair about it and retrain people, not just drop them. I'd keep it reasonable, I'm not a ranter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the timesheets, fuel cards and rota are the exact things AI would do. The planning software would probably do the rota better than me. I'd be worried they'd keep Henrik and one admin, and I'm the newer one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a couple of people at work had tried the new tools and they worked, I'd learn them properly. I'd ask Henrik if I could learn the compliance side, like driver hours rules and vehicle checks, because that's harder to hand to software. And we'd slow down on the house, maybe wait a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, then properly worried when I think about the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the house wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because you don't take on a mortgage when your job might shrink. Lukas earns a bit more than me, but we'd want both wages safe. Waiting a year feels sensible, not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the software would do the rota better. Does that sting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I've been trying to get good at the rota for a year. Watching a program do the driver rota in ten seconds would make me wonder what I've been doing for a year.

say: It's **change**, and we'd have to adapt like everyone.
Firms should **retrain** people fairly, not just **drop them**.
think: Timesheets, fuel cards and the **rota** are exactly what AI would do.
If they keep one admin, I'm the **newer one**.
do: Learn the new tools once **colleagues** prove they work.
Ask Henrik to train me in **compliance**: driver hours and vehicle checks.
Push the **house purchase** back by about a year.
S1.quote: Watching a program do the driver rota in ten seconds would make me wonder what I've been doing for a year.
fieldNote: Her pride is tied to the **rota**, which software would do instantly.
She delays the **house** as a sensible step, not panic.
Compliance work is her chosen **safer corner**.

steps.text: Learn the planning software once colleagues have tested it
Ask Henrik for training on driver hours and vehicle checks
Push the house purchase back by a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and companies should get help to keep people on while they work it out. Like the support during the pandemic. I'd say it at work and at my parents' dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, my office job goes by 2028. The thing that scares me more is Lukas, because he runs a warehouse team and robots come for that around 2031. So it's me first, then him three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house plan completely and keep all the savings as cash. I'd look for work that's hands-on, maybe in the Brandt workshop or as a driver, because I've got a car licence and could do the lorry licence. And I'd use the AI tools at work to stay useful until they let me go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd feel like the ground was moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A lorry licence? Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drivers always say there's a shortage, and Henrik would help me get the licence. Driving is hands-on, so it gets the extra three years. I don't love the idea of nights away, but it beats nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lukas say to each other?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd say we're lucky to have savings and no kids yet. Then Lukas (her partner) and I would make a spreadsheet, because that's what we do. I'd feel better with the numbers in front of me.

say: Two years is **too fast**, and firms need help to keep people on the **payroll**.
We need support like during the **pandemic**, said at work and at home.
think: My office job at Brandt Haulage **goes by 2028**, whatever I do.
Lukas's **warehouse team** follows three years later, when robots come around **2031**.
do: Stop the **house plan** and keep all savings as cash.
Get a **lorry licence** with Henrik's help.
Use AI tools at work to **stay useful** until let go.
S2.quote: We'd say we're lucky to have savings and no kids yet. Then Lukas (her partner) and I would make a spreadsheet, because that's what we do.
fieldNote: She sees a **two-step** household loss: her desk, then her partner's warehouse.
A **lorry licence** is a practical, hands-on fallback within her firm.
**Numbers** calm her; the spreadsheet is her coping habit.

steps.text: Cancel the house plan and hold savings as cash
Train for a lorry licence with Henrik's help
Use the firm's AI tools daily to stay useful

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if firms are straight with people. I'd want Brandt Haulage to say clearly what's changing and when. Sensible stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 32 when it lands. Five years is enough to get a lorry licence and some driving experience, so I'd go into 2031 with a hands-on job. Lukas and I would still be worried about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd learn the AI tools at work properly, once others had. In year two I'd get the lorry licence and start doing some driving shifts. We'd buy a smaller house than planned, with a mortgage Lukas could cover alone if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd have a plan, so it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to do it in order, instead of all at once. With five years I'd get the lorry licence while I still had the office pay. In the two-year picture I'd be scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And 2034, when robots can drive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what we'd do. We'd have savings and maybe a house half paid. I'd hope there's something new by then.

say: Five years is **enough** to get ready if firms are **straight** with people.
Brandt Haulage should say clearly **what changes** and when.
think: I'd be **32** when it lands, ideally already driving a lorry.
Lukas and I would still worry about **2034**, when robots can drive and lift.
do: Learn the **AI tools** once others have.
Get a **lorry licence** in year two and take driving shifts.
Buy a **smaller house** Lukas could cover alone.
S3.quote: With five years I'd get the lorry licence while I still had the office pay. In the two-year picture I'd be scrambling.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **sequence** steps instead of scrambling.
Her mortgage rule: a house **one wage** can cover.
She is honest that **2034** has no answer yet.

steps.text: Learn the firm's AI tools after colleagues have
Get a lorry licence and take driving shifts in year two
Buy a smaller house one wage can cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and people will cope. I'd say firms should plan training now, so nobody's caught out. Very middle of the road, that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel okay. I'd be 37, the house would be bought, and I'd have time to find something that lasts. I'd still keep an eye on Lukas's warehouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house on the original plan. I'd stay at Brandt and get good at the compliance side over a few years, then look around year five at what's actually happening. I'd keep about six months saved at all times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Uneasy now and then when I see the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until year five to look around?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want to see what's proven. Lots of things get announced and don't happen. By year five you'd know which jobs are really safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever start something of your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small rota and paperwork service for little haulage firms, if I got good. But that's thinking work too, so it would only last until 2036. I'd keep it small.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, and people will cope.
Firms should **plan training** now so nobody's caught out.
think: At 37, with the **house bought**, I'd have time to find something lasting.
I'd still keep an eye on Lukas's **warehouse** job.
do: Buy the **house** on the original plan.
Get good at **compliance** work at Brandt over a few years.
Keep **six months** of savings at all times.
feel: Mostly **calm**, **uneasy** now and then at the news.
S4.quote: Lots of things get announced and don't happen. By year five you'd know which jobs are really safe.
fieldNote: She waits for **proof**, true to her steady nature.
The **house** goes ahead on the original timeline.
A side business idea is dismissed as **thinking work** that wouldn't last.

steps.text: Buy the house on the original two-year timeline
Train in compliance work at Brandt Haulage
Keep six months of savings as a floor

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's me and then Lukas, one after the other, with no time in between. What would help is firms getting support to keep people on while they retrain, and help paying for things like a lorry licence.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners' jobs together. I kept thinking about Lukas more than me. My office job goes first, then Lukas (her partner) loses his warehouse team three years later. Two wages going one after the other is the real fear.

headlineQuote: My office job goes first, then Lukas (her partner) loses his warehouse team three years later. Two wages going one after the other is the real fear.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old** junior admin at Brandt Haulage, a trucking firm, still learning the **driver rota**.
She uses AI now and then and waits for **colleagues** to prove new tools.
She and partner Lukas are **saving for a house**, and every scenario reshapes that plan.
Her fallback is a **lorry licence**, a hands-on job inside the same firm.
Her deepest fear is **two household wages** falling one after the other.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, with her job then her partner's **warehouse** job going.
whatWouldHelp: Support for firms to **keep people on** while they retrain.
Help paying for **licences** like the lorry licence.
